name: Ab wheel

lead: An ab wheel (ab roller) is a small wheel on an axle with handles on either side. The user kneels or stands, grips the handles and rolls the wheel forward until the body is extended, then pulls back.

It is used to train the abdominal wall and anti-extension strength of the trunk. In looksmaxxing it is promoted for visible abs, but visibility is reported to depend mainly on low body fat; the wheel trains the muscle underneath.

paras: As the wheel rolls out, the lever arm grows and the abdominal muscles must resist the spine arching toward extension, loading the rectus abdominis, obliques and deep core, with the lats and shoulders also working. Electromyography studies of similar rollout devices show high abdominal activity, although no peer-reviewed study of the standard kneeling rollout alone was located.

Lower-back sag, shoulder strain and wrist discomfort are the common problems, and the exercise is difficult for many beginners without partial range or a wall stop. People with back or shoulder issues are generally advised to take care. Marketing that the wheel flattens the stomach is not supported by research: spot training has not been shown to reliably reduce fat from one area.

lead: An ab wheel, also called an ab roller, is a small wheel (or pair of wheels) on an axle with a handle on each side. The user typically kneels, grips the handles, rolls the wheel forward while keeping the spine straight, and rolls back to the start [1]. The movement is described as an anti-extension exercise, meaning the trunk muscles work to resist the lower back arching as the lever arm lengthens [1].

It is used to train the rectus abdominis, internal and external obliques and transverse abdominis, with the lower back, lats and shoulders also contributing [1]. In looksmaxxing discussion it is associated with developing visible abdominal muscles. Proponents and fitness writers commonly note that how visible the abs are depends heavily on body-fat level, so the wheel is framed as building the muscle rather than removing fat above it.

The device is inexpensive and portable. One machine-written source describes the modern Ab Roller, launched in 1994 and sold via infomercials, as one of the best-selling fitness products of all time [1]. Published research on the standard rollout specifically is thin, although electromyographic comparisons of abdominal exercises have been published [2].
infobox: Ab Roller, 1994 (inventor reported as Don Brown) [1]

paras: Basic components are a wheel, an axle and handles. Wheels are generally rubber or plastic with a textured tread, axles are steel, and handles carry foam or rubber grips [1]. Some models include sealed bearings for smoother rolling [1].

Dual-wheel designs have two wheels side by side on a shared axle and are described as more stable laterally, which makes them more forgiving for beginners [1]. Single-wheel designs require more balance and are described as harder [1]. Some products add a return spring or a knee pad.

According to one source, wheel-based exercise devices were patented in the 1930s, mainly for lower-back exercises, and a commercial product called the Reduce-A-Wheel appeared in the United States in the 1960s [1]. The Abdominizer, a non-wheel device invented in 1984 by a Canadian chiropractor, is cited as another earlier abdominal product [1].

The same source dates the modern Ab Roller to 1994 and credits its popularity to mid-1990s infomercials, with the manufacturer claiming more than 10 million units sold and over $1 billion in revenue [1]. These dates and figures come from a machine-written encyclopedia and have not been independently verified.

As the wheel moves away from the body, the lever arm grows and the abdominal muscles must resist the trunk extending. This loads the rectus abdominis, obliques and deep abdominal muscles, with the shoulders and lats stabilising and controlling the return [1]. Range of motion, starting position (kneeling versus standing) and wheel design change the difficulty.

A 2006 study in Physical Therapy used electromyography to compare traditional and non-traditional abdominal exercises, with implications for training and rehabilitation [2]. Wider fitness-writing sources describe ab wheel rollouts as producing higher abdominal muscle activation than some traditional exercises [1], but no peer-reviewed study of the plain kneeling rollout was identified in the material reviewed.

Researchers on fat loss have reported that fat is not reliably reduced from a specific area by exercising the muscle beneath it, so changes in how visible the abdominal muscles are depend mainly on overall body fat. This is a general finding about exercise, not a result specific to the ab wheel.

Commonly reported problems include lower-back sagging into extension, shoulder strain and wrist discomfort. The exercise is demanding, and beginners often use a shortened range, a wall stop or a dual-wheel model. People with back or shoulder conditions are generally advised by trainers to be cautious. One source asserts that proper use reduces back-injury risk by training spinal stabilisation [1]; that claim has not been tested in trials identified here.
No studies found on the ab wheel as a product for appearance outcomes. A related laboratory study compared electromyographic activity across traditional and non-traditional abdominal exercises [2].

The ab wheel is discussed as an inexpensive way to train the abdominal wall at home. The common framing in fitness communities is that the muscle can be developed with training but that visible definition depends on diet and body fat. Community-specific material was not available for detailed documentation.

timeline.event: Wheel-based exercise devices for lower-back work are reported to be patented [1].
The Reduce-A-Wheel is reported as an early commercial ab-wheel-like product in the United States [1].
The Ab Roller is introduced and later sold widely through infomercials [1].
